decision.reasoning:
EXPECTED VIEWS × FULL-WATCH RETENTION decides it, and Palomares wins on both.

1) STORY ENGINE AND RETENTION. This is the only finalist with a real ticking clock (an 80-day hunt with Soviet trawlers and the world press watching), a payoff (the bomb comes up on 7 Apr) and a sting after the payoff (the plutonium is still in the soil and the fence is still up). Its reversals are physical events, not paperwork: mid-air collision, then plutonium rain, then the fisherman's sighting with nothing to point at but open water, then the largest naval search to date with Bayesian probability maps, then the ambassador's swim, then FOUND, then the line parts and the bomb is LOST AGAIN for 9 days, then it is re-found, CURV gets snagged, and the bomb is lifted, then the contamination twist. That gives 8–9 peaks across 14–20 minutes, which fits the 'so many climaxes' brief.
- The Louvre's back half is procedural (hearings, audits, empty searches). By design it has no resolution and no protagonist, so retention would fall off a cliff after minute 5.
- Bull has a great one-two in the middle (assassination, then the Teesport pipes), but the main whodunit can never be answered, the HARP opening is slow, and the climax is a 1996 report.

2) DEMAND AND CTR CEILING. 'Lost nuke' is a proven multi-million genre:
- Infographics 3.04M, Timeline 2.68M, Thoughty2 2.64M, Herrera 2.63M, SkyFury 8.24M and Kyle Hill 5.97M as recent nuclear breakouts.
- Videos specifically about Palomares top out at 808K. The genre has demand, but there is no definitive telling of this story yet.
- The Louvre has bigger raw demand, but it is badly saturated. Primal Space, SML, Zoufry, Hank Green and about 30 low-effort uploads already have the 3D rebuild, and our own revised forecast for it is only 120–400K.
- Bull's 'underserved' claim turned out to be false: Real Engineering has 2.58M and Qxir 611K already covers Teesport and Britain's role.
- Palomares is the only one where our angle, a bomb lost twice, is both fresh and the strongest beat in the story.

3) PACKAGING. 'America Lost the Same H-Bomb Twice' has a familiar noun, an absurd premise and a proven '…Twice' shape. 'H-Bomb' instead of 'Nuke' separates it from the Goldsboro '…Nuked…Twice' videos.
- 'WHERE'S #4?' (three bombs and a red dashed gap) reads in under 1 s at 168×94. It complements the title rather than repeating it: the image says there were four and one is gone, and the title says it was lost twice.
- It works worldwide. Bull's packaging leans on the UK ('Sheffield', 'Teesport'), and the Louvre's leads depend on fact gates for the expert recutting quotes.

4) FACT SAFETY. Palomares is the lowest-risk option: a 1967 Navy report, Moran's book, the 1975 DNA report, the NYT 2016 piece, and no living people accused.
- The Louvre is the highest-risk: an active case with suspects charged but not convicted, and the jewels could be recovered at any moment, which would break the title.
- Bull's killing can only ever be 'suspected'.

5) VISUAL TOOLKIT. Palomares fits it best: a painted blue-sky Spanish coast, a vertical sea cutaway, a yellow Alvin lighting a white B28 in its parachute, a Bayesian probability grid lighting up cell by cell, a split-flap counter for DAY 1 → DAY 80, Navy report pages, and the fenced field. Every peak is a diorama we can build with no real likenesses needed.

6) LANE RULE. Cold War disaster / deep-sea search thriller is a new lane after two money and markets episodes. It is not a repeat of the Hormuz geopolitics episode either.

What we lose:
- The 60th anniversary (Jan 2026) has passed, so the video has to be evergreen and win on Browse from the lost-nukes cluster.
- The genre is crowded, which is why the lead package must push the 'twice' angle hard and show a better telling inside 30 s (probability grid plus a primary Navy record on screen, never stock B-52 footage).
- Realistic base: CTR at or above the channel median +1 pt and 2–4× the channel median views at 28 days. The 2.6–3M+ genre ceiling (and the 10M stretch) is reachable only if the 24 Mar line-snap sequence holds retention past the midpoint.

finalists.title: The Day America Lost a Hydrogen Bomb
finalists.pitch: LANE: Cold War disaster / deep-sea search thriller. ANGLE: in 1966 the US dropped four H-bombs on a Spanish fishing village and found three. The fourth was seen only by a fisherman nobody believed, and it took an 80-day hunt with a tiny submarine. The bomb slipped away a second time, and the plutonium is still in the soil. HOOK: 'On January 17th, 1966, four hydrogen bombs fell out of the sky over a Spanish village called Palomares. Three of them landed. The fourth disappeared, and the only man who saw where it went was a fisherman nobody would listen to.' SPINE: (1) A Chrome Dome B-52 collides with its KC-135 during refuelling at 31,000 ft; 7 die. (2) Four bombs fall. One lands softly in a riverbed, and in two the conventional explosives detonate, spraying plutonium on tomato fields. (3) Bomb No. 4 is missing. Francisco Simó Orts ('Paco de la Bomba') saw a parachute go into the sea, but the search stays on land. (4) Escalation: the largest naval search to date, probability maps (an early landmark use of Bayesian search), dozens of ships, Alvin. (5) PR stunt: the US ambassador swims on camera. (6) FOUND (15 Mar): Alvin sees the parachute ~2,550 ft down on a steep slope. (7) REVERSAL (24 Mar): the lift line fails and the bomb slides deeper. (8) Found again, the CURV robot gets tangled, and the bomb is lifted on 7 Apr, day 80. (9) TWIST: 1,400 tons of soil shipped to South Carolina, but land is still fenced, the 2015 US–Spain cleanup pledge was never carried out, and cleanup airmen later reported illness (NYT 2016). CLIMAXES: mid-air collision; plutonium rain; fisherman ignored; ambassador's swim; Alvin finds it; line snaps; robot tangled then recovery; contamination still there. HERO OBJECT: white B28 casing on a grey seabed slope wrapped in its parachute, lit by Alvin's lamps. THUMBNAIL: bright vertical cutaway with a sunny Spanish coast and a tiny fishing boat on top, and deep below the bomb in its parachute with yellow Alvin approaching. Red loop on the bomb. Text 'BOMB #4' / 'STILL LOST?'. DEMAND: Infographics 'Live Nuke Still Missing' 3.04M, Timeline 2.68M, Thoughty2 2.64M, Fascinating Horror Goldsboro 1.14M, Wendigang 969K, LazerPig 919K. Palomares-specific videos top out at 808K (History Guy) / 173K, so it is underserved. Nuclear near-miss breakouts this year: SkyFury 8.24M, Kyle Hill SL-1 5.97M. 60th-anniversary interest in 2026. SOURCES: Barbara Moran 'The Day We Lost the H-Bomb' (2009); US Navy 'Aircraft Salvage Operation Mediterranean' (1967); DNA Palomares Summary Report (1975); NYT Dave Philipps 19 Jun 2016; WHOI Alvin records; 2015 US–Spain statement of intent; CIEMAT monitoring; Beyond Nuclear (Apr 2026). FACT RISK: LOW-MEDIUM. Lock depths and dates to the Navy report and confirm the crew toll split. Present the airmen's health as 'veterans say / NYT reported'. Confirm the cleanup status against Spanish reporting. Say 'one of the first big uses' of Bayesian search, not 'invented'.

kills: Familiar topic: Palomares is already covered by Infographics Show, Timeline, Thoughty2 and the 2026 copycats. Anyone who has seen one of those reads 'lost nuke Spain' as a rerun. Only the 'lost it again' angle is fresh, and the packaging has to push it hard.

Lead thumbnail fails at phone size. A thin rope with a frayed end is about 2 px wide at 168×94, so the 'snapped' story you are paying for disappears. The red loop then circles nothing you can read. What's left looks like a white cylinder under a pale blob: a buoy, a jellyfish or a diver. It does not read as a nuke.
The lead is written as a 'vertical frame'. Thumbnails are 16:9. If it gets painted portrait and cropped, the ship, the line and the bomb won't all fit at a readable scale.
A nose-down bomb with its parachute trailing upward looks like it is sinking slowly, not falling away. The motion doesn't read as 'they dropped it'.

'America Lost the Same Nuke Twice' is strong but a little cute. A viewer who knows the story will feel the second loss was a 9-day hiccup, which makes the title an overclaim. 'America Lost an H-Bomb. Then Lost It Again' is clearer and reads more honest. 'They Found the Lost Nuke. Then It Slipped' is the weakest: 'slipped' is soft.

The hook is a spoiler summary. It names four bombs, the riverbed, the plutonium, the fisherman, two months, the find and the loss. That is the whole movie trailer in 25 seconds, all in the same flat declarative rhythm. Almost every sentence carries the beat, but I already have the plot, so why stay?
'One fisherman sees exactly where' goes nowhere. There's no conflict attached, so it's a dead open loop.
'The worst part of this story isn't in the sea at all' is vague. Every YouTube hook ends with 'and the worst part…'. Without a concrete image it rolls my eyes rather than pulling me in.
There's no date and no human cost. Seven airmen died and that isn't mentioned, so the crash feels like a cartoon rather than real.

finalists.title: The Man Who Built a Gun to Shoot Into Space
finalists.pitch: LANE: engineering / unsolved assassination. ANGLE: a Canadian ballistics genius nearly fired satellites into orbit from a cannon. Rejected by the West, he built Saddam a 1-metre-bore 'supergun' and was shot dead at his own front door. Three weeks later British customs found the barrel disguised as oil pipes. HOOK: 'In 1966 one man fired a shell from a cannon 180 kilometres straight up, to the edge of space. Twenty-four years later he was shot five times outside his Brussels apartment, and three weeks after that British customs found the reason inside a crate of oil pipes.' SPINE: (1) Project HARP: a 16-inch naval gun in Barbados throws a projectile to ~180 km, a record. (2) Canada and the US pull funding, and the dream dies. (3) Hero to felon: shells to apartheid South Africa break an embargo, and he is jailed in the US in 1980. (4) 1988, the Saddam deal: Project Babylon, a ~150 m gun, with 'Baby Babylon' built. (5) Warnings and apartment break-ins, then 22 Mar 1990: five shots at his door, ~$20K cash untouched. A professional hit, never solved. (6) Teesport, three weeks later: the giant 'petrochemical pipes' are the supergun barrel. (7) TWIST: the Arms-to-Iraq / Matrix Churchill scandal and the 1996 Scott Report show British ministers knew far more than they admitted. CLIMAXES: a cannon to the edge of space; funding pulled; hero becomes felon; the Saddam contract; assassination at his door; the 'oil pipes' at Teesport; the UK government knew. HERO OBJECT: a giant barrel aimed at the sky, assembled from pipe sections stamped with shipping labels. THUMBNAIL: bright blue-sky diorama with a skyscraper-length gun climbing a hillside, a tiny suited figure beneath it, a shell streaking to space. Text 'HE ALMOST DID IT'. DEMAND: underserved (Qxir 611K top, Banijay 315K, Megaprojects 172K; the Teesport angle has barely any coverage). Analogs: fern Azorian 5.53M, Dark Docs stolen MiG-25 1.73M. A unique lane (engineering + geopolitics + whodunit) with an iconic oversized object for 3D. SOURCES: Scott Report (1996); William Lowther 'Arms and the Man' (1991); McGill/HARP records; NYT/BBC 1990 coverage of the killing and the Teesport seizure. FACT RISK: MEDIUM. The killing is unsolved, so Mossad or Iraq involvement is 'suspected' only. Use Scott Report dimensions. The 1980 guilty plea is fact.

He had about twenty thousand dollars on him. [beat] His killer left it. [beat] And two years before this crate was opened, a British MP had warned the government exactly what these pipes were. finalists.pitch: LANE: heist / crime reconstruction plus a one-year-on mystery. ANGLE: the world's most famous museum was beaten by a furniture lift and two scooters. The film starts as a second-by-second 3D rebuild of the Apollo Gallery and turns into an investigation. The thieves are in jail but the jewels have vanished, and the only modern precedent for getting stolen crown jewels back (Dresden 2022) needed a plea deal. HOOK: 'On a Sunday morning, four men in hi-vis vests rode a furniture lift up the side of the most visited museum on Earth and took France's crown jewels in under eight minutes. A year later police have caught the men. They have not found a single jewel.' SPINE: (1) Cold open on the 1911 Mona Lisa theft as a bookend. (2) 19 Oct 2025, 9:30am: a truck-mounted lift on Quai François-Mitterrand, a disc cutter through the balcony window, two cases smashed, 8 pieces taken, gone on scooters in about 7 minutes (split-flap timer). (3) REVERSAL: they drop Empress Eugénie's crown, which is found crushed on the pavement. (4) The security autopsy: des Cars tells the Senate the only facade camera faced away from the balcony. The Cour des comptes finds delayed upgrades (about €3M of an estimated €83M plan invested 2018–24). The 2014 ANSSI audit 'LOUVRE' password is attributed to Libération and is NOT shown to have been in use in 2025. The parliamentary inquiry finds 'systemic failures' and the director resigns in Feb 2026. (5) The hunt: DNA on the lift, an arrest at CDG with a one-way ticket, the network widening to Aubervilliers. (6) REVERSAL: about 100 investigators search homes, cellars and attics and find nothing. The last CCTV trace is a lock-up in the same suburb, and the suspects point to an unnamed 'ringleader' that investigators doubt. (7) The Dresden precedent: jewels came back only through a plea deal, and the Dresden White is still gone. (8) ENDING: three futures shown as split dioramas: a deal, a fence (Antwerp, Tel Aviv, India), or the cutting wheel. Interpol says stolen objects resurface anywhere from 3 months to 40 years later. CLIMAXES: lift and window cut; crown dropped; camera pointed the wrong way; password claim; CDG arrest; director resigns; searches come up empty; Dresden plea-deal precedent; final fork. HERO OBJECT: Eugénie's crushed crown under a glass dome with an empty velvet tray, and the furniture lift on the facade behind. THUMBNAIL: bright 3D Louvre Seine facade on blue sky, a yellow/red lift at the open window, a gold crown falling mid-air, red loop on the window. Text 'STILL MISSING' (alt '7 MINUTES' plus a split-flap €88,000,000). DEMAND: the strongest proven demand on the list. Primal Space 4.83M, SML 4.74M, Zoufry 3.48M, Hank Green 2.77M, Josh Johnson 2.33M, CBC 2.07M. The museum-heist ceiling is BuzzFeed Gardner at 10.67M. Live peg: France 24/AFP one-year pieces (19 Oct 2026) and the Prime Video 'Masterplan' heist film. Gap: no definitive spatial reconstruction that also covers the security failures, the resignation, the empty searches and the Dresden precedent. SOURCES: Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau statements (AP/Reuters/Le Monde/ABC); Senate culture committee hearing of des Cars (22 Oct 2025); Cour des comptes report (Nov 2025); parliamentary inquiry and resignation (The National, 25 Feb 2026); Libération on the 2014 ANSSI audit; France 24 one-year reports (19 Oct 2026); Artnet on the Dresden verdict. FACT RISK: MEDIUM-HIGH. Suspects are charged (mis en examen), not convicted, so no names and status words throughout. Use 'about €88M (curators' estimate)'. Re-check the counts of people held and the jewel status on VO day. Present the 'destroyed' scenario as an expert scenario, not fact. Note the lane overlap with the Remmo/Dresden candidate, which is used here as a sub-beat instead.
